record.paper_title: Protocols for Observational Studies: Methods and Open Problems
record.original_question: In matched observational studies, when researchers must decide whether to specify the study protocol before or after matching treated and control units, what methods besides prespecifying important matching covariates before matching can reduce researcher hope bias, where researcher hope bias means understating uncertainty or declining to match on possible confounders because the researcher hopes the matched study will retain enough power to be informative?

evidence.quote: For specifying before vs. after the match, the potential of researcher hope bias (understatement of uncertainty from specifying a protocol after matching because the researcher hopes it will be feasible to learn something useful from the data) needs to be traded off against the information one can learn about unmeasured confounding from specifying a protocol after matching.

One potential way to reduce researcher hope bias is to before matching, specify the list of covariates that are thought to be important to match on and provide reasons in the final protocol for any changes from this initial list [15]. It would be useful if future work could provide other ways of reducing researcher hope bias.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a matched observational study in which a researcher matches treated units to control units on observed covariates and then performs outcome analysis to test a causal hypothesis. The researcher must decide whether to fully specify the study protocol (including the choice of matching covariates, calipers, balance constraints, test statistics, and inference procedures) before performing the matching or after inspecting the matched sample. Define "researcher hope bias" as the tendency, when specifying (or revising) a protocol after matching, to understate uncertainty or to decline to match on possible confounders because the researcher hopes that the resulting matched study will retain enough statistical power to be informative.

One known mitigation is the following: before matching, the researcher specifies a list of covariates believed to be important to match on, and in the final protocol provides explicit reasons for any deviations from this initial list.

Problem: Devise and rigorously justify additional methodologies — beyond prespecification of an initial covariate list with documented deviations — that provably reduce researcher hope bias in matched observational studies, while still allowing the researcher to use information learned from the matched sample (e.g., about unmeasured confounding) when finalizing the protocol. A satisfactory answer should describe the procedure, the statistical guarantees it provides (for example, on Type I error, coverage, or sensitivity-analysis validity), and the assumptions required.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as an explicit open methodological problem in the literature on protocols for matched observational studies. A brief web search did not surface a definitive subsequent methodology that comprehensively addresses researcher hope bias beyond the prespecified-covariate-list approach. Related work on preregistration, sample splitting, and design-based sensitivity analysis exists but does not appear to claim resolution of this problem.

status_evidence.title: Protocols for Observational Studies: Methods and Open Problems
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses trade-offs between specifying protocols before vs. after matching and flags researcher hope bias as a concern needing further methodological work.
status_evidence.claim: The problem of finding additional ways to reduce researcher hope bias in matched observational studies is posed as open.
